The Matterhorn is an iconic Alpine peak at fourteen thousand six hundred ninety-two feet on the Switzerland-Italy border, famous for its distinctive pyramidal form and treacherous rock. Located in the Pennine Alps near Zermatt, Switzerland, the pyramid shape and dramatic exposed rock make it visually striking and instantly recognizable, with minimal glaciers at this elevation. The first ascent on July fourteenth, eighteen sixty-five, by Edward Whymper and his party of seven ended in tragedy when four climbers fell to their deaths on descent. Among the dead were climber Robert Hadow and guide Michel Croz, and this event shocked Victorian Europe, launching the mountain into cultural legend as a symbol of mountaineering ambition and peril. The accident galvanized debate about the ethics of mountaineering and the role of guides and remains the most famous climbing tragedy of the era. Climbs typically take one to two days. The normal route from Zermatt is non-technical scrambling but exposed and requires surefootedness and acclimatization. Loose rock and poor weather claim twelve to fifteen climbers per year, making the mountain notoriously dangerous despite its modest elevation. Over three thousand climbers attempt the peak annually, with the small season window from June through September concentrating traffic and hazard.
